data.text:
HOW CHINA FEASTS ON WAR

The world braced for Hormuz to close.

Yet the tankers keep sailing.

Millions of barrels are heading toward China.

You think Iran can afford to cut off their war budget to spite Uncle Sam?

Iran's economy runs on oil exports. And China is its largest buyer. Even under sanctions. In some ways, especially under sanctions.

So the message to Beijing: "We are fighting the West. Not you."

Iranian foreign minister now speaks about the strait as if it remains open by grace, like a favor Iran is extending to the world.

Truth is that a total closure would destroy them, too. Iran would isolate itself instantly.

So instead of closing Hormuz, they squeeze it.

Pressure with favoritism.

Ships tied to Western economies face threats, inspections, insurance nightmares; whilr tankers toward a "friend" quietly keep moving.

Toll booth, really. Toll booth with missiles, but toll booth. The US, Israel: maybe they take the long way around.

That is extraordinary leverage. For a country under sanctions. One skinny waterway. A giant pressure valve on the entire global economy.

At times, shipping traffic through Hormuz has nearly collapsed. Not necessarily to literal zero but close. Oil markets don't wait for ships to burn. They panic on rumor.

The strait is usually described as an energy chokepoint. It is also a chokepoint for labor.

When we say roughly 20 percent of the world's oil passes through Hormuz, they never talk about the guys actually steering the damn ships.

A remarkable number of them come from the Philippines.

Filipino sailors are everywhere in global shipping. Officers, engineers, deckhands, quietly embedded in the world trade. The Philippines is not at war in the Gulf. But Filipino sailors are sailing through it every day.

Now missiles circle those waters and the tankers still sail.

The Philippines doesn't control the oil system. But Filipinos help operate it. Remove them, oil stops flowing. If Filipino labor powers the system, why does Manila behaves like it has no seat at the energy table?

Some ships are trying a new trick. Vessels in the gulf have started broadcasting strange messages on their tracking systems. "China owner." A little electronic sign saying: Hey missiles, relax, we're friendly.

Beijing plays a careful double game. China calls for negotiations and restraint even as it continues to purchase Iranian crude. Every tanker bound for Chinese refineries pumps revenue to Tehran's economy.

China sends no troops. Beijing trades with all sides: Iran, Saudi, Israel, gulf states. Tries to avoid looking like a military ally of Tehran.

If at all, Beijing doesn't need warships in the Gulf; war is already delivering what it wants.

But it sends money. And money sustains wars. Diplomatic cover. As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, Beijing can veto resolutions calling for harsher sanctions or international intervention.

That means Iran knows something important: The world's most powerful diplomatic body cannot easily move against it without China's consent.

Many people think the Middle East oil wars are about America securing energy.

But sanctions have created a stranger system.

When producers like Iran, Russia, Venezuela are cut off from Western markets, their customer list shrinks. Prices drop. China doesn't need to control oil fields in Iran. It simply needs to be the buyer of last resort when everyone else leaves the market. So the barrels still move, just east instead of west.

Discounted oil. Fewer competitors. A world where sanctioned producers have fewer places to sell.

That's a much cheaper form of influence.
